title: Nest vocabulary: the words before the wiring

questions.prompt: You're adding "a customer can't have more than 3 open orders". Which file?

options.text: The service — it's a business rule, and services hold the work
The controller, right after reading the body
The module, since it decides what's allowed
A decorator on the route

questions.explanation: The controller's job is translation: read the request, call something, return the result. Rules that would still be true if the request arrived from a queue or a cron job belong in the service — that's what makes them testable without HTTP and reusable from a second entry point.

questions.prompt: What's the relationship between a "service" and a "provider"?

options.text: Provider is the general term for anything the injector can hand out; a service is the most common kind
They're two words for exactly the same thing
A provider provides HTTP routes; a service provides data
A provider is a module that exports a service

questions.explanation: Every service is a provider; not every provider is a service. A config object, a database connection or a fake for tests can all be providers — they're just things registered in a module's `providers` array so the injector can hand them out.

questions.prompt: When does the `@Get(":id")` decorator actually run?

options.text: Once, when the class is first loaded — it attaches metadata Nest reads to build its route table
On every matching request, just before the method
Never — it's stripped by TypeScript, like a type
Only at build time; it doesn't exist at runtime

questions.explanation: A decorator is a function that runs once at class-definition time and leaves a note (metadata) behind. Nest reads those notes at startup to learn which URL maps to which method. The *method* is what runs per request — which is why putting expensive work "in a decorator" isn't a thing.

questions.prompt: `@Controller("users")` on the class, `@Post(":id/orders")` on the method. What URL does that answer?

options.text: POST /users/:id/orders
POST /:id/orders
POST /users
Both /users and /:id/orders, as two routes

questions.explanation: The controller prefix and the method path are glued together — that's all a "sub-route" is. `:id` is a route parameter: it matches any segment there, and `@Param("id")` pulls the matched text out.

questions.prompt: A client wants to change only an order's `note` field, leaving everything else alone. Which verb?

options.text: PATCH — a partial update of an existing resource
PUT — it's an update
POST — it's a write
GET with the new value in the query string

questions.explanation: `PUT` means "replace the whole resource" — send a PUT with only `note` and a strict server should blank the other fields. `PATCH` means "apply this change". `POST` is for creating or for actions that aren't safe to repeat, and `GET` must never change anything (browsers, proxies and prefetchers all assume that).

questions.prompt: `@Param("id") id: string` gets `/users/42`. What's in `id`, and why does the type say `string`?

options.text: The text `"42"` — a URL carries only text, so everything from the path or query arrives as a string until a pipe converts it
The number 42; TypeScript coerces it from the annotation
An object `{ id: "42" }`
`undefined`, unless the route declares a type

questions.explanation: TypeScript annotations are erased at runtime — they never convert anything. `"42"` stays a string until something at runtime parses it, which is exactly the job of a pipe (`ParseIntPipe`, or the global `ValidationPipe` with `transform: true`).

questions.prompt: What does `constructor(private readonly users: UsersService) {}` do, beyond taking an argument?

options.text: It declares a field and assigns the argument to it — `this.users` is available in every method
Nothing extra; `private` is only documentation
It creates a new `UsersService` for this class
It registers `UsersService` with the module

questions.explanation: It's a TypeScript *parameter property*: `private readonly x: T` in a constructor is shorthand for declaring the field, taking the argument, and doing `this.x = x`. `private`/`readonly` are compile-time only — they express intent and are erased at runtime. Note what it doesn't do: no `new`, and no registration. The class only *declares* what it needs; the module registers, and the injector supplies.

questions.prompt: A service sets `this.currentUser = user` at the top of a method, awaits a DB call, then reads `this.currentUser`. What's wrong?

options.text: The provider is a singleton — one object shared by all requests — so a concurrent request can overwrite the field during the await
Nothing; each request gets its own instance by default
The field should have been `readonly`
Only a typing issue — the field needs `| undefined`

questions.explanation: Node serves requests concurrently on one thread: at every `await`, another request can run and reassign the field. Fields on a provider are for application-lifetime things (a connection, config, a cache); request-specific data should stay in arguments and return values, where it can't be clobbered.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what separates a guard from an interceptor?

options.text: A guard decides yes/no before the handler; an interceptor wraps the handler and can also change what comes back
Guards are for auth; interceptors are for logging — nothing else is possible
Nothing structural; they just run in a different order
A guard is async, an interceptor is synchronous

questions.explanation: The contracts say it: `canActivate()` answers with a boolean — or a `Promise`/`Observable` of one, so it can await a token check — while `intercept(context, next)` gets a handle on the rest of the chain, so it runs code before *and* after and can transform the response. Both can be async; the difference is structural, not timing. That's why authorization is a guard and a `{ data }` envelope is an interceptor.

questions.prompt: Why does a guard write `context.switchToHttp().getRequest()` instead of just taking `req`?

options.text: `ExecutionContext` is transport-agnostic — the same class can run for HTTP, WebSockets or microservice messages, so you say which world you're in
It's a performance optimization — the request is built lazily
It sanitizes the request first
It converts the Express request into a Fastify one

questions.explanation: Guards, interceptors and filters run in every transport Nest supports, so the context is an envelope around "whatever is being handled", with `switchToHttp()` / `switchToWs()` / `switchToRpc()` to unwrap it. It also exposes `getHandler()` and `getClass()`, which is how a guard reads route metadata such as `@Roles("admin")`.

prompts.prompt: Mark this class as something the injector may create and hand out.
prompts.explanation: `@Injectable()` marks a class as available to the injector. It still has to be listed in a module's `providers` array — the decorator describes, the module registers. Note the parentheses: the decorator is a function call.

prompts.prompt: Answer `GET /users/42`: the class prefix, the verb decorator with a route parameter, and the decorator that reads it.
prompts.explanation: Prefix + method path = the full route, so this is `/users/:id`. `@Param("id")` pulls the matched segment out as a **string** — `"42"`, not `42`.

prompts.prompt: Create an order from the request's JSON body.
prompts.explanation: `POST` is the verb for creating a resource (repeat it and you get two orders — that's expected). `@Body()` hands you the parsed JSON. On its own it does **no** checking: the `CreateOrderDto` annotation is erased at runtime, so validating the shape is a pipe's job.

prompts.prompt: Give this controller the service in one line — declared, never constructed.
prompts.explanation: `private readonly users: UsersService` is a parameter property: it declares the field, takes the argument, and assigns it. `this` is the object the method was called on, so `this.users` is the instance the injector supplied — not one this class created.

prompts.prompt: Register the controller and the service for this feature.
prompts.explanation: `controllers` are the HTTP entry points; `providers` are the things the injector can build and hand out inside this module. Forgetting the `providers` entry is the classic cause of "Nest can't resolve dependencies of the UsersController".

prompts.prompt: Reach the HTTP request from inside a guard.
prompts.explanation: `ExecutionContext` wraps whatever is being handled — an HTTP request, a WebSocket message, an RPC call — so you unwrap it with `switchToHttp()` (or `switchToWs()` / `switchToRpc()`). Returning `false` from `canActivate` makes Nest answer 403.
